title: AI Agents vs. Agentic AI: A Conceptual Taxonomy, Applications and Challenges
extended_summary:
This paper addresses a conceptual question rather than an educational intervention question: how AI Agents differ from Agentic AI, and how these paradigms can be organized into a structured taxonomy. The authors review prior literature to distinguish single-agent, tool-augmented systems from more autonomous multi-agent systems, and they discuss architectural evolution, application areas, and technical challenges such as hallucination, brittleness, coordination failure, and explainability.

The paper’s approach is a narrative/conceptual review supported by a hybrid literature search across academic databases and AI-assisted search tools. It does not report an experiment, intervention, or outcome study in schools. Instead, it synthesizes definitions, compares paradigms such as generative AI, AI agents, and agentic AI, and proposes comparative frameworks spanning autonomy, architecture, memory, planning, interaction, and application scope.

No participant population is studied. The examples are drawn from domains such as customer support, enterprise search, robotics, medical decision support, research automation, and smart home systems. Although ChatGPT and related LLM systems are discussed as enabling technologies, the paper does not describe any high-school, secondary, or writing-related ChatGPT trial, and it does not report any 25-plus-25 student experiment, 12-week intervention, motivation outcomes, writing scores, random assignment, or effect sizes.

The main conclusion is that AI Agents and Agentic AI should be treated as distinct but related paradigms: AI Agents are generally single-entity, tool-using systems for bounded tasks, while Agentic AI involves multiple specialized agents coordinating toward broader goals. For the present evidence-verification task, this paper is not the alleged 2026 motivation randomized controlled trial and provides no usable quantitative evidence for synthesis on ChatGPT-based writing feedback in high school. It should therefore be excluded from any quantitative synthesis of such interventions because it is not a primary educational outcome study.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/review paper on AI agents and agentic AI, not an empirical education study. It contains no K-12 intervention evaluation, no randomized or quasi-experimental design, no writing or motivation outcomes, and no extractable original statistics relevant to ChatGPT-based writing feedback.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not report any direct educational impact estimates. Its relevance to the alleged high-school ChatGPT writing RCT is only indirect and conceptual, so impact on educational outcomes is unclear and not quantifiable.
